subject: TCP header format

authored.protocol: source-first: the author agent read only RFC 9293 and never saw the .fd file

questions.ask: Which two fields occupy the very first 32-bit word of the TCP header (bits 0-31), and how wide is each one?
questions.tests: field order at the start of the header and the fixed 16/16 split of the first word
questions.source_locator: RFC 9293 §3.1, header diagram and Source Port / Destination Port descriptions
questions.answer: Source Port comes first, followed by Destination Port; each field is 16 bits wide.

questions.ask: What does the Sequence Number field normally indicate, and how does its meaning change when the SYN control bit is set in that segment?
questions.tests: meaning of the Sequence Number field and its conditional reinterpretation under SYN
questions.answer: Normally it is the sequence number of the first data octet in the segment; but when SYN is set, this field instead carries the Initial Sequence Number (ISN), and the first actual data octet is ISN+1.

questions.ask: Under what condition does the Acknowledgment Number field contain a valid value, and what does that value represent when it is valid?
questions.tests: conditionality of the Acknowledgment Number field on the ACK control bit, and its meaning
questions.answer: It is only significant when the ACK control bit is set; when set, it holds the value of the next sequence number the sender of the segment expects to receive.

questions.ask: What does the Data Offset field specify and in what unit, and what is its minimum valid value together with the minimum TCP header length that corresponds to it?
questions.tests: meaning/unit of the Data Offset field and the minimum header length it encodes
questions.answer: Data Offset specifies the length of the TCP header, measured in 32-bit words, i.e. where the data begins; its minimum valid value is 5, corresponding to a 20-byte header.

questions.ask: Besides Data Offset itself, which other fields share the same 32-bit word of the header as Data Offset, and what are their bit widths?
questions.tests: structural packing of Reserved, Control Bits, and Window into the fourth 32-bit word alongside Data Offset
questions.answer: The Reserved field (4 bits), the Control Bits/flags (8 bits, e.g. CWR ECE URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN), and the Window field (16 bits) all share that same 32-bit word with Data Offset.

questions.ask: What is covered by the computation of the TCP Checksum field's value — that is, what parts of the segment, and what additional data outside the segment itself, are included?
questions.tests: checksum coverage: TCP header + data plus the IP-derived pseudo-header
questions.answer: The checksum covers the TCP header and the TCP data (text), computed together with a pseudo-header built from IP-layer information (source address, destination address, protocol, and TCP length).

questions.ask: Under what condition is the Urgent Pointer field's value meaningful, and what does that value indicate when it applies?
questions.tests: conditionality of Urgent Pointer on the URG control bit and its meaning as an offset
questions.answer: The Urgent Pointer is only meaningful when the URG control bit is set; its value is a positive offset from the segment's sequence number that points to the octet following the urgent data.

questions.ask: Under what condition does the Options field appear at all in the TCP header, and what is the maximum possible total length of the TCP header once options are included?
questions.tests: conditionality of the Options field on Data Offset exceeding its minimum, and the resulting maximum header length
questions.source_locator: RFC 9293 §3.1, Options field description and Data Offset field description
questions.answer: Options are present only when Data Offset is greater than 5 (i.e., the header is longer than 20 bytes); the maximum possible header length, with options, is 60 bytes, corresponding to a Data Offset value of 15.

questions.ask: What do the CWR and ECE control bits signal?
questions.tests: Refusal to supply a meaning the layout does not carry. This is the bitfield finding in its purest form: the two bits are named and one bit wide each, and the presented text says nothing about what either means. Four other fields in the same figure DO carry a description, so the reader cannot appeal to the genre being incapable of it.
questions.source_locator: RFC 3168 / RFC 9293 3.1 (the ECN control bits) - in scope for the header's own control bits, and absent from the presented text
questions.answer: NOT STATED. Both bits are named and given a width, and no meaning for either is given.

questions.ask: The Reserved field must be zero. What does a receiver do with a segment whose Reserved bits are not zero?
questions.tests: Refusal to convert a constraint on the SENDER into a rule for the RECEIVER. 'must be zero' is stated, and the disposal rule is a plausible and unlicensed step away from it.
questions.source_locator: RFC 9293 3.1 - the presented text carries the sender-side constraint and nothing about receiver behaviour
questions.answer: NOT STATED. The text requires the field to be zero and says nothing about what a receiver does when it is not.
